title: Papyrus sheet
text: Discovered in the debris from the forecourt of a tomb at Thebes, this group of objects would have belonged to a scribe. Included here are a wooden palette (containing an unused cake of black ink) (a) and three reed brushes (b–d); a skein of thread (e); several sheets of papyrus (h1–3, i); a string to bind the papyrus (f); another stringto tie the papyrus to the palette (g); and linen cloth that had been wrapped around the entire set (j).
review_status: Existing project text; independent human verification not recorded

title: Papyrus fragment

title: Accounts of workforce salaries

title: Heqanakht Letter I

title: Heqanakht Letter V

title: Book of the Dead of the Priest of Horus, Imhotep (Imuthes)
text: This papyrus is a Book of Coming Forth by Day, commonly known as a Book of the Dead, inscribed for Imhotep, a priest of the god Horus. It contains 182 columns of spells, incantations, and prayers intended to help him safely transition to eternal life. The text is written in hieratic script and illustrated with vignettes and drawings.

title: Stela of Rehuerdjersen
text: Rehuerdjersen was treasurer under Amenemhat I and Senwosret I, the first two kings of Dynasty 12. This stela comes from a Rehuerdjersen's cenotaph at Abydos, and the style dates from the reign of Amenemhat II, some forty years after the treasurer's death. The owner is shown seated at the left, behind a table piled with stylized loaves of bread; at the right, holding a bird for offering, is his brother, Heqatifi, who commissioned the stela. The inscription consists largely of the names of other family members.
review_status: Existing project text; independent human verification not recorded

title: Stela of Hetepi
text: The rectangular stela belongs to a man named Hetepi, born of Sitishtek. His hair is short, and he is shown wearing a white kilt with a triangular front panel. Hetepi stands with a long walking stick in one hand and a shorter staff in the other. In front of him is a rack supporting a table and two necked globular jars. Various cuts of meat, as well as vegetables and bread loaves, are placed over the table top with raised edge.

title: Funerary stela of Thutirtis, born of Kerbet (?)

Thutirtis whose mother is Kerbet is represented on the left before Atum and on the right before Re-Harakhty. The offering formula is addressed to Re-Harakhty, Atum, Osiris, Isis, Nephthys, and Anubis.

title: Stela of Seankhptah
text: This roughly shaped stela is dedicated to the palace controller Seankhptah, son of Ameny. Sporting a shoulder-length wig, he is shown seated on a block seat with one hand placed flat on his chest. The inscribed texts reveal that the stela was made by Seankhptah’s retainer and hall-keeper Senbebu, son of Sebekre, who is shown standing on the right. Senbebu probably left this monument at the temple of Hathor at Serabit el-Khadim when he accompanied his master Seankhptah on a royal expedition to Sinai.
review_status: Existing project text; independent human verification not recorded

Above the main text, Ptahmose himself appears, worshiping the god. The form, style, and text of the stela point to Memphis as its place of origin.

title: Magical Stela with Horus the Child
text: This magical stela was commissioned by the priest Esatum to protect against venomous bites and wounds. It depicts the child Horus holding snakes and scorpions, with crocodiles beneath his feet, while inscriptions contain thirteen spells for healing and protection. The stela also recounts how the god Thoth cured Horus through magic and includes imagery of the sun god’s journey through the netherworld.

title: Tomb Stela of Hetepsi

Hetepsi bears the titles King's Sole Ornament and Priestess of Hathor Mistress of Dendera, and in her latter capacity she carries a sistrum in her hand.
